findings.where: Phone first screen, inside the hero frame: the order photo, caption, headline, yellow address strip, then the 'I advise multilateral development banks…' paragraph
findings.fault: On a phone, the line saying what Mark does and who he does it for comes after the email strip and falls below the first screen. A visitor sees his face, an opinion and an email address before learning that he advises development banks and governments. The desktop hero puts this paragraph before the action.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank staff member who opens the site on a phone from a LinkedIn link. They want to know within seconds whether this advisor works for bodies like theirs, and on the first screen the only clue is the credential line. Mark would object as well, because his ask comes before his reason.

findings.where: First screen, desktop: the overall arrangement of large light serif text on the left half and a tight studio headshot filling the right
findings.fault: The hero uses the common law-firm and consultancy pattern: a text half beside a headshot half. The hairline frame is too faint to register and the yellow strip is small, so at a glance nothing makes the page his own. The large quiet paper above the headline adds to the generic, subdued feel.
findings.who_objects: The founder. The brief fails 'a look any consultancy could own' and asks for 'alive, not boring' after round 1's dull v5. A visitor would not remember this page apart from other advisors' sites.

findings.where: Nav bar (Profile · Articles · Blog), desktop and phone
findings.fault: The nav has no 'Contact' item. The only route to Mark is the address strip on the home hero, so on any deeper page the nav gives no visible way to reach him.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who arrives on an article from a social post and wants to write to him. First-visit trust resolves 'a clear way to get in touch' with a Contact label in the navigation and the address in every footer, and this tile shows neither.

findings.where: Article specimen, the 'Download' block after the article's closing line
findings.fault: A 2024 blog post on PPP law ends with a 'Download' label and a link to a different piece, a 2026 lecture on streamlining the PPP process. Nothing says how the two are related, so the label reads as 'download this article' while the title says otherwise. On desktop, the 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF' line is pushed to the far right, away from the title it describes.
findings.who_objects: A reader who expects the PDF of what they just read and gets another document. The brief calls the PDF list 'the product', so a list that is confusing at its first item undercuts it.

findings.where: First screen: the headline 'public-private partnerships' against the paragraph just below it, 'Public-Private Partnerships'
findings.fault: The same term is lower case in the headline and capitalised in the paragraph directly under it, so the first screen looks unedited.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, a lawyer or a bank official, who notices the term set two ways inside one glance. Mark, as a lawyer, would want the defined term written one way.

findings.where: Palette, the Pad yellow swatch: 'The address strip, selected text'
findings.fault: The yellow is given a second job as the text-selection colour. The brief keeps it to one place only, behind one quotation or the contact panel, as a colour memory.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for the legal-pad yellow to be used once and with restraint. As a selection colour it shows up wherever a reader highlights text.

findings.fault: This part is a button (parts.txt), but it uses the blue underlined look the page keeps for links. It acts on this page but looks as if it goes somewhere.
findings.who_objects: A reviewer checking the tile, who expects an underlined blue line to navigate. The page's one link look ends up meaning two functions.
